title: Tolla and the Talkative Stick
markdown:
In the soaring peaks of Cragtop, where the wind whispered secrets through ancient pine forests and rope bridges swayed like nervous ribbons between dizzying cliffs, lived a goblin named Tolla. She wasn’t just any goblin. Her eyes, as bright as polished emeralds, shimmered with endless curiosity. Her mind spun with clever, sometimes slightly wild, plans. Her home was a cozy cavern, lit by fireflies held in crystal jars, and the air smelled of damp earth and roasted mushrooms.

Tolla’s biggest worry, like most goblins in Cragtop, was a constant argument with the Grimbles. These practical folk lived in homes dug right into the steep cliffs. Their grand quarrel was all about the most delicious mountain berries. Goblins claimed they found them first, with quick feet and sharp eyes in the lower meadows. Grimbles insisted their higher homes and climbing gear gave them first dibs on the plumpest berries on the sunniest ledges. This berry battle was as old as the mountains themselves. Sometimes it even involved who could sing the loudest mountain songs. Tolla, with a deep sigh that stirred dust motes dancing in her cavern, decided it was time to settle this with a flourish of dignity and an exceptional offering.

Tolla’s plan was simple, elegant, and full of her usual flair. She would gather the finest sun-berries, plump and blushing with ripeness. She would then preserve them in sweet, glistening dew collected from moonpetal flowers. This would make them gleam like tiny rubies, perfect for presenting. Next, she would journey along the dizzying rope bridges connecting the goblin caves to the Grimbles’ cliffside homes, carrying this magnificent offering as a gesture of goodwill. “This,” Tolla declared to the flickering lamplight, her voice full of hopeful resolve, “will be a grand success in making peace! Dignity and deliciousness, hand in hand, will finally bridge the berry-divide!”

With a determined nod that made her pointed ears twitch, Tolla gathered a wicker basket overflowing with the glistening berries. She carefully arranged them, ensuring each ruby-like orb was perfectly placed. Then she slung a worn but sturdy walking stick over her shoulder. This was Elderbranch, a piece of ancient mountain ash. Its wood was gnarled and smoothed by countless journeys, seeming to hold the whispers of forgotten winds and the silent stories of the mountains.

The first bridge was familiar and thrilling. Wind tugged her patched cloak. Mist below like a grey blanket. Cliffside lanterns, hung by generations, shimmered on wet stone. On a particularly wobbly stretch, ropes creaking a mournful tune, a dry raspy voice arrived unnervingly close to her ear.

“Honestly, Tolla, must we take this particular bridge? Far too breezy. My bark is practically freezing. A distinct draft in my very core. Not good for long-term structural integrity.”

Tolla froze, heart leaping. Elderbranch had, in recent years, developed a vocal personality, as if the wood had absorbed so much mountain chatter it had grown opinions.

“Elderbranch, not now.” She shuffled forward with extra caution.

“Not now? And when is a good time for a walking stick to voice professional opinions on arboreal comfort and airborne humidity? This peace-offering business is ridiculous. Grimbles are stubborn. They’ll stare at your sugary offerings and wonder if they can patch cave walls with them.” A pause, dry leaves skittering. “And these berries are likely not properly ripened. They probably squish. A true berry needs a firm bite and a satisfying pop.”

Tolla’s knuckles whitened on the stick. “It’s diplomacy. Showing we can share.”

“Share their grumbling? Their cave décor that looks like piles of damp moss? I recall you complaining about their rock-music last festival. Sounded like grumpy cave trolls falling down a well. And these berries spent too much time in the shade. A proper berry needs sunlight. Lots of it. Like me, leaning against a sunny rock.”

She pressed on, resolve tested by every gust and every exasperated word. The path steepened toward jagged dwellings carved into sheer face like colossal owl nests. The higher they climbed, the more Elderbranch found fault.

“My joints ache. The altitude is appalling for woody integrity. Far too thin. That goat track looks less precipitous. More suited to sensible sticks with a healthy regard for their own well-being.”

At the cavern entrance — a gaping maw — Grimbles peered out with wary beady eyes. A burly one, beard like a mossy waterfall, arms thick as trunks, stepped forward.

“What brings a goblin to our doorstep, Tolla? Haven’t seen one this far up since the Great Berry Scuffle of ’ought-eight.”

Tolla held up the basket, still gleaming. “Greetings, respected Grimbles. A token of peace: our finest sun-berries, preserved by moonpetal dew.”

Before she could bow, Elderbranch boomed, cavern acoustics turning it into an insult with an echo. “Fine, you call them? Distinctly mediocre! Amateurish cultivation. You shove them in dirt and hope. A proper berry needs sun-dappled soil, a gentle misting, and a well-balanced diet of more sensible berries. I’ve seen better specimens on a poorly maintained fence post in the goblin market. And they probably tasted better too.”

Stunned silence. Beards bristled. The burly Grimble’s fists looked capable of crushing boulders. “Insolence! You insult our berries, goblin. Our traditions. Our honour. Are you here to mock us with dewdrops and half-baked opinions disguised as gifts?”

Tolla’s heart sank. Dignity vanished like morning mist. Rock-hammers were coming off belts. This was not the ending she had packed the basket for.

Then a sunbeam of an idea, slightly mad. She stepped forward, emerald eyes mischievous, voice theatrical.

“Mock you? Oh, no.” She took Elderbranch off her shoulder, cradled it like a precious artefact, held it out. “It is not I who speaks with such discerning critique, but my esteemed companion, Elderbranch. No ordinary stick. A diplomat of great experience. A scholar of all things verdant.”

She improvised, imagination soaring. “He has travelled far, observing flora and cultivation. He finds your methods fascinating. He believes you are on the cusp of a revolutionary technique he’s only read about in ancient botanical scrolls.” A conspiratorial whisper. “And he insists on staying, here, in your magnificent caverns, to impart his vast, albeit highly critical, knowledge. Consider him a gift. A consultant. A wooden advisor. Legendary status. Epic, even.”

The Grimbles stared. A talking stick. A consultant. Anger wobbled into bafflement. Elderbranch, relishing the attention, grumbled on.

“Consultant? I am a well-travelled arboreal authority, thank you. These berries are still questionable. Where’s the sunlight? All shadow and damp. Are you rotating the soil? I doubt it. And the watering schedule — don’t even get me started.”

To Tolla’s astonishment, a chuckle started as a rumble and grew into hearty bellows. The burly Grimble scratched his mossy beard, grinning. “A talking stick, eh? More talkative than old Gnarledroot after fermented moss-wine.” He eyed Elderbranch, now lecturing a bewildered listener on root aeration. “Perhaps he does have ideas. Our berries have been a bit predictable. A little commentary never hurt. All right, goblin. We’ll accept your stick. More interesting than another argument about first pick of the brambles. If he learns us a thing or two about berries, all the better. We like learning. Especially if it involves food.”

Tolla bowed deeply, a wide smile spreading across her face, luck barely believed. “A wise decision, indeed!” With a final exasperated glance at Elderbranch, who was now demonstrating the proper technique for soil turning using its own wood, she turned and made her way back down the cliff. She walked with a lighter step, the basket now empty, her heart full of laughter and the sweet scent of an unexpectedly peaceful resolution. The feud wasn’t settled with solemn dignity, but with a healthy dose of goblin resourcefulness and a rather vocal, opinionated piece of wood. As she descended, leaving the Grimbles to their new talkative advisor, the mountain — always full of surprises — had just become a little funnier. The Grimbles had a consultant. Tolla had the walk home, and the wind, for once, had nothing to add.
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for older children
